citizen.blurb: The moment a trained AI puts what it learned to work for you.
citizen.standfirst: What actually happens between typing a message and getting a reply, and why that one step, not training, is the one you pay for every single time.
citizen.core:
A trained AI model is like a chef who went to cooking school. The school taught the chef recipes, skills, and methods. That is training. It takes a long time and shapes what the chef knows.

When a customer orders food, the chef does not learn to cook again. The chef uses what they already know to make that meal. That is inference: the model uses what it learned to answer a new request.

Training and inference are two different stages. Training is rare and can take weeks and a lot of computing power. Inference happens each time the model is used. Every chat reply, generated image, or autocomplete result needs inference.

A common mistake is to think the model learns from each chat. In a normal chat, it does not. It reads your input and creates a reply from what it learned during training. The model itself does not change.
citizen.everyday:
Each time you ask a chatbot a question and get a reply, you trigger inference. The model does not search for your exact question in a database. It builds the answer step by step from patterns learned during training.

This is why it can answer a question it has not seen in that exact form. It is also why it can sound sure and still be wrong. It creates a likely answer from patterns instead of checking every fact first.

A chat can only use earlier messages if the app sends them back to the model. Each new request is still a new inference.
citizen.businesses:
If your company uses an AI API, each call is inference. Vendors often charge based on how much text goes in and comes out. The cost grows with use.

A support bot that answers 10,000 questions a day may run 10,000 inference requests each day. That makes inference an ongoing cost.

This matters when you plan an AI feature. Building or tuning a model may cost money up front. Running it costs money again and again. A small pilot may be cheap, but the same feature can cost much more at scale. Estimate normal traffic and busy periods before you commit.
citizen.appBuilders:
Every model API call in your app is inference. Training or fine-tuning is a separate step.

Your design choices affect both cost and speed. Longer prompts, more chat history, and longer replies usually need more computing. Shorter prompts and less old chat can lower the bill. At scale, small savings can add up.
citizen.modelBuilders:
Choices made during training can affect how fast and costly inference will be later. Bigger models may perform better, but they often cost more and run more slowly.

Builders may shrink or simplify a model after training so it is cheaper to run. At large scale, a smaller and faster model can be more useful than a slightly better model that costs too much.
citizen.smalltalk: Training teaches the AI; inference is the AI using what it learned to answer you now.

technical.blurb: A forward pass through a trained model's fixed weights, run once per generated token.
technical.standfirst: Autoregressive decoding, KV caching, token-based cost and latency scaling, batching trade-offs, and quantization — the mechanics that decide whether inference is fast and cheap or slow and expensive.
technical.core:
Inference is running a trained model's forward pass on a specific input to produce an output, with the model's weights held fixed. This is distinct from training, where the same forward pass is followed by a backward pass: backpropagation computes gradients, and an optimizer like Adam or SGD updates the weights based on those gradients. Inference only does the forward half; nothing about the model changes as a result of running it.

For autoregressive language models, inference isn't a single forward pass but a loop: the model predicts one token, appends it to the sequence, and runs another forward pass conditioned on the extended sequence, repeating until it emits a stop token or hits a length limit. A common misconception among engineers newer to LLM serving is treating an inference call as a single fixed-cost operation like a typical API request. It isn't: an inference request's latency and compute cost scale roughly linearly with the number of tokens generated, because each token requires its own forward pass through the network, and a request asking for a 2,000-token response takes meaningfully longer and costs meaningfully more than one asking for 50 tokens.
technical.appBuilders:
Every API call to a hosted LLM is an inference request, priced and rate-limited by token count, not by request count alone. Input tokens (your prompt, system message, and any retrieved context) and output tokens (the generated response) are typically billed separately, and output tokens usually cost more per token because they each require a full forward pass, while input tokens can be processed in parallel in a single pass.

Two levers matter most in practice. First, context length: everything you put in the prompt — chat history, retrieved documents, tool definitions — counts against the model's context window and adds to input-token cost and prefill latency. Second, generation length: capping max output tokens, or prompting the model toward concise answers, directly reduces both cost and time-to-completion. If you're building a latency-sensitive feature, know that time-to-first-token (dominated by prefill, i.e., processing the input) and time-per-output-token (dominated by the decode loop) are different metrics with different bottlenecks, and providers often report them separately.
technical.businesses:
Inference is the recurring operational cost of an AI feature, distinct from the one-time or periodic cost of training or fine-tuning a model. At meaningful scale, inference cost typically dominates total cost of ownership for an LLM-based product, since it recurs on every user interaction indefinitely, while training happens once or occasionally.

Capacity planning for inference differs from planning for typical stateless web services because GPU-backed inference has different scaling economics: batching improves throughput per GPU but adds queuing latency, and providers typically offer a latency/cost trade-off through tiers (e.g., standard versus low-latency or "priority" endpoints, or self-hosting with techniques like quantization to fit more concurrent requests per GPU). Evaluating a vendor or self-hosting decision should account for sustained inference volume, not just the cost of an initial pilot, since per-request pricing multiplies directly with usage growth.
technical.modelBuilders: Model builders make architecture and training choices that determine inference cost for the model's entire deployed lifetime: parameter count, attention mechanism (e.g., grouped-query attention reduces KV-cache memory versus standard multi-head attention), and numerical precision all trade off inference speed and memory against output quality. Techniques like distillation, pruning, and post-training quantization are applied specifically to reduce inference cost after a larger model has already been trained, since a smaller or lower-precision model is cheaper and faster to serve even if it took less compute to produce than the original.
technical.smalltalk: Training is the model learning once; inference is it doing the actual work — one token at a time — every time you send it a prompt.
